prompt: In a blue/green deployment that has just failed, how is the traffic returned to the old version?
hint: Is the old version still running?

choices.text: The old image is rebuilt and deployed again, task by task
choices.why: That is how a rolling deployment rolls back; blue/green keeps the old tasks alive.

choices.text: ECS restores the service from its last snapshot
choices.why: ECS keeps no snapshot of a service; the old task set is simply still running.

choices.text: The listener moves back to the blue target group
choices.why: Right. Blue never stopped, so returning is a listener change.

choices.text: DNS is pointed at the old load balancer
choices.why: One load balancer serves both; only its listener changes target group.

prompt: What does blue/green cost that a rolling deployment does not?
hint: Count the tasks running at the busiest moment.

choices.text: A second load balancer for green
choices.why: Both target groups sit behind the same load balancer.

choices.text: Double capacity while blue is kept
choices.why: Right. A full green set runs beside blue until blue is terminated.

choices.text: A longer outage while the listener switches
choices.why: The switch is a listener change, with no outage; that is the point of it.

choices.text: A database copy for the green tasks
choices.why: Both versions share the database, which is why the rollback section matters.

prompt: Match each CodeDeploy configuration to what it does with the traffic.
hint: Read the name: percentage, then time.

pairs.right: Everything to green in one move
10% first, the rest after five minutes

right_distractors: Tasks replaced a few at a time, with no green set

prompt: What is the test listener on 8443 for, in the shop's deployment group?
hint: Who reaches green before customers do?

choices.text: A smoke test reaches green before any customer
choices.why: Right. The AfterAllowTestTraffic hook runs against it.

choices.text: It carries the canary's 10% of customer traffic
choices.why: The canary's share goes through the production listener; the test one carries no customers.

choices.text: It lets an administrator reach blue during the switch
choices.why: It routes to green, not blue: the new version, before release.

choices.text: It is the port the load balancer's health checks use
choices.why: Health checks go to the targets directly, not through a listener.

prompt: moto returned the deployment group with an empty `alarmConfiguration`. On AWS, what mistake has the same effect?
hint: An alarm that is accepted and never fires.

choices.text: Listing more than two alarms
choices.why: A group can list several alarms; the number is not the problem.

choices.text: Turning on DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM
choices.why: That is what makes an alarm roll back; it does not remove one.

choices.text: Using CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce
choices.why: The strategy does not change whether the alarms exist.

choices.text: Naming an alarm with a typo, or one that lives in another region
choices.why: Right. The group accepts the name and watches an alarm that never goes into ALARM.

prompt: `terminationWaitTimeInMinutes` is 60. A problem is found 90 minutes after a successful deployment. How quick is the rollback?

choices.text: Seconds: the listener moves back to blue
choices.why: Blue was terminated at minute 60; there is nothing to move back to.

choices.text: It is a new deployment of the old version
choices.why: Right. After the wait, a rollback is a full deployment like any other.

choices.text: Impossible: CodeDeploy refuses to deploy an older task definition
choices.why: Any task definition can be deployed; older is not refused.

choices.text: Instant, because CodeDeploy keeps blue until the next release
choices.why: Blue is kept for the wait time and no longer.

prompt: In the model, a 10% canary watched by an alarm on the whole service failed 500 requests, more than all at once. Why?
hint: Divide the canary's errors by all the traffic.

choices.text: The canary sends 10% of traffic to a version that is 10% slower
choices.why: The model has no latency at all; it counts failures.

choices.text: Diluted to 2%, the errors never crossed the threshold until everything shifted
choices.why: Right. 10% of 20% is 2%, not above 2%, so the alarm waited for the full shift.

choices.text: Canaries always fail more requests than an all-at-once release
choices.why: With the alarm on the new version, the same canary failed 40.

choices.text: CodeDeploy pauses alarms during the canary window
choices.why: Nothing is paused; the alarm saw a rate at the threshold, not above it.

prompt: A release fails 8% of its requests. During a 10% canary, what error rate, in percent, does an alarm on the whole service see?
Which metric lets an alarm watch only the green task set on ECS behind an Application Load Balancer?
hint: Blue and green each have their own target group.

choices.text: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count for the load balancer
choices.why: That counts errors the load balancer itself produced, for every target group at once.

choices.text: CPUUtilization of the ECS cluster
choices.why: CPU says nothing about failed requests, and covers both versions.

choices.text: HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count with the green target group as dimension
choices.why: Right. Per target group, it counts the new version's errors alone.

choices.text: RequestCount for the whole load balancer
choices.why: A request count is not an error count, and this one mixes both versions.

choices.text: A copy of the algorithm CodeDeploy uses to shift traffic
choices.why: It is nobody's algorithm; it plays a simple bad release through four assumptions.

choices.text: A Lambda hook that runs after test traffic is allowed
choices.why: The hook in the AppSpec is a separate function; canary.py runs on your laptop.

choices.text: A script that reads CodeDeploy's metrics from moto
choices.why: It calls nothing at all; every number in it is an input you can change.

choices.text: A model with stated assumptions, not CodeDeploy
choices.why: Right. moto runs no deployment, so the lesson counts with a model and says so.

prompt: Release 1.4.1 renamed a column and started using the new name. The canary alarm fires and traffic returns to 1.4.0. What happens next?
hint: Does a rollback touch the database?

choices.text: 1.4.0 fails, asking for a column that no longer exists
choices.why: Right. The rollback worked and the service is down in both versions.

choices.text: 1.4.0 serves normally, because the rollback restored the schema
choices.why: A rollback moves traffic; the renamed column stays renamed.

choices.text: CodeDeploy refuses the rollback because the schema changed
choices.why: CodeDeploy knows nothing of databases and does not check.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as terminationWaitTimeInMinutes has not passed
choices.why: The wait keeps blue's tasks, not the old schema.

prompt: Put the three releases of a safe column rename in order.
items: Add the new column and write to both
Copy the old values and switch reads to the new column
Drop the old column once nothing reads it
trap: Switching reads before the copy is the slip: rows written earlier would read as empty.

prompt: The three-release way to change a schema so every step can be rolled back is called expand and ___.
Which of these does a blue/green rollback restore? Choose all that apply.
hint: It restores what the old task set was running.

choices.text: The image the old task definition names
choices.why: Yes. The old tasks still run it.

choices.text: A parameter changed in Parameter Store with the release
choices.why: No. A value outside the task definition stays as it was set.

choices.text: The environment variables in the old task definition
choices.why: Yes. They are part of the task definition the old tasks run.

choices.text: Rows the new version wrote to the database
choices.why: No. Data written stays written; that is the rollback's limit.

prompt: A release can fail by being slow rather than by returning errors. What should the deployment group carry to catch that?
hint: A second symptom needs a second alarm.

choices.text: A longer canary window, so slowness has time to become errors
choices.why: Slowness may never become errors, and customers suffer it meanwhile.

choices.text: A smaller canary share, 1% instead of 10%
choices.why: A smaller share reduces exposure and evidence; it does not detect slowness.

choices.text: A latency alarm on the green target group
choices.why: Right. That is why the shop's group names api-green-p99 beside api-green-5xx.

choices.text: The ECSAllAtOnce configuration, so the problem is obvious at once
choices.why: Obvious to every customer at once is the outcome a canary exists to avoid.

prompt: At 2,000 requests a minute, a release fails 30% of its requests. A canary sends it 10% for 3 minutes before the alarm rolls it back. How many requests failed?
hint: Requests times share times failure rate times minutes.
